newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans tumble ahead of big harvest weekend.
newsitem.headline: Soybeans tumble ahead of big harvest weekend.

text.p: Soybean prices collapsed Friday with traders expecting farmers to begin the season's first major harvest this weekend.
An unexpected rise in usage gave cocoa prices a sharp boost while lumber rose for the fourth consecutive day amid indications a slump in cash demand may be over.

Forecasts call for hot, dry weather this weekend from Iowa to Ohio and, if accurate, combines should take a large bite out of the U.S. soybean crop. The crop is large; the Department of Agriculture estimates it at 2.27 billion bushels vs. 2.15 billion a year ago.
Some private analysts say the crop may amount to as much as 2.30 billion bushels.
"There is no mystery here. There's a good crop coming on," said Steve Bruce, analyst with E.D. and F. Man International.

Farmers have been anxious to harvest because the crop is late due to a wet spring and a cool summer. The Agriculture Department said 4 percent of the crop was harvested as of Monday vs. 12 percent a year ago and an average of 15 percent.

"It looks pretty good for harvesting activity in the corn belt," said Fred Gesser, chief forecaster for Weather Express Inc. Gesser predicted 70-degree weather in the western Midwest Saturday and the entire region Sunday.
Forecasts for scattered showers next week also had farmers anxious to get started while fields are dry.
Chicago Board of Trade November soybeans closed down 10-1/4 cents, a third of the daily 30-cent limit, at $7.27-1/4 per bushel, the lowest close since July 26.
Cocoa at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange ended higher, bolstered by a strong European third quarter usage.
Cocoa grindings, a key indicator of consumption, rocketed 42 percent to 48,855 metric tons in Britain during the third quarter vs. a year ago. Industry analysts had expected a 20 percent increase.
Third-quarter Dutch grindings rose 16 percent to 99,549 tons vs. analysts' forecasts for a 10 percent increase.
"The grind numbers for 1996 are higher because of better consumption due to cooler weather," Merrilly Lynch analyst Judith Ganes said.
Benchmark CSCE December cocoa rose $9 a ton to $1,351.
Reports that cash prices may have reached a bottom fuelled buying of Chicago Mercantile Exchange lumber futures with prices ending sharply higher for the fourth consecutive day, traders said.
Random Lengths quoted cash spruce down $1.00 at $366 per thousand board feet for the week, but analysts noted the decline had slowed. Cash prices have tumbled $66 since mid-September.
Traders said higher bond prices, signalling lower interest rates, could boost home sales and lumber demand.
CME November lumber rose $7.40 to $358.40. The daily price limit is $10.

Heating oil closed lower at the New York Mercantile Exchange, ending consecutive sessions of strong gains. As they did on the way up, crude oil and gasoline followed heating oil back down, traders said.

"The market took a little breather today," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst at Cargill Investor Services in New York. "The market is going to look very closely at heating oil, and will be very sensitive to weather."

Heating oil for November delivery ended Friday 0.26 cent lower at 74.43 cents a gallon. Crude oil for November delivery dropped 8 cents to $24.73 a barrel and November gasoline fell 0.05 cent at 63.63 cents a gallon.
